language_wrapper: In a math contest, {n} numbered seats are arranged around a circular table. A subset S of these seats is called admissible if |S| = {k} and, in every block of {w} consecutive seats around the circle, at most {s} of them lie in S. How many admissible subsets are there?
hardness_rationale: Compared to the seed problem (linear arrangement, no 3 consecutive selections, any size), this family simultaneously (i) moves to a circular arrangement with wrap-around constraints, (ii) replaces the simple 'no three consecutive' rule by a general sliding-window cap: in any block of w consecutive positions, at most s may be chosen, and (iii) requires counting only subsets of exact cardinality k. The circular wrap-around plus fixed-cardinality constraint forces a transfer-matrix/dynamic programming treatment over an automaton of size 2^(w-1), tracking both state and the total number of ones. This eliminates simple tribonacci-like recurrences and guessing; even small instances require careful state-based reasoning and counting of closed walks.
notes: Proof idea and correctness: Encode admissible subsets as binary sequences a_1,...,a_n on a circle, where a_i = 1 iff i ∈ S. The constraint 'in every block of w consecutive seats, at most s selections' translates to: for each i, sum(a_i, a_{i+1}, ..., a_{i+w-1}) ≤ s, indices modulo n. Consider the automaton whose states are all (w-1)-bit contexts u ∈ {0,1}^{w-1}, representing the last w-1 bits before the next position. From a state u, appending b ∈ {0,1} is allowed iff popcount(u) + b ≤ s; the new state is the shift of u with b appended. Traversing the circle corresponds to taking n such transitions; each transition represents exactly one length-w window, so the constraint is enforced edge-wise. A labeled circular sequence corresponds to a closed walk of length n (start and end at the same state) and contributes one unit to the count for the unique start context equal to the (w-1) bits preceding position 1. Tracking the number of ones is handled by summing the b labels along the walk; requiring |S| = k becomes counting closed walks with total weight k. Thus, the number of admissible subsets equals the sum, over all states s, of the number of closed walks of length n from s back to s with total appended ones k. The verifier implements exactly this DP: dp_t[u][m] counts walks of length t ending at state u with m ones; initialization dp_0[start][0] = 1 for each start, and transitions add either b=0 or b=1 as allowed. The final answer is sum_s dp_n[s][k]. The global density bound w·k ≤ s·n is checked to rule out impossible k. Difficulty enforcement ensures instances where both choices (0 and 1) are possible at some states and the count is nontrivial. This approach is robust, avoids undefined operations, and scales well for w ≤ 6 and n up to around 80.
source_question: Choose a subset of integers from 1 to 15 such that no three consecutive integers are in the chosen set (you can choose an empty set). How many different sets are there?
